dossier:
I read Anthropic’s “Effective Harnesses for Long-Running Agents.” The source is not a full execution transcript; it is an engineering post describing repeated observed behavior from Claude/Opus 4.5 running in the Claude Agent SDK over multiple context windows. The chronological account below is limited to what the post reports.

## Chronological account of the failure

### 1. Initial setup and assignment

Anthropic describes running Claude Opus 4.5 “on the Claude Agent SDK in a loop across multiple context windows.” The agent was given only a high-level software-building prompt, exemplified as:

> “build a clone of claude.ai”

The intended outcome was a production-quality web app. The harness had normal Claude Agent SDK capabilities: the agent could use tools to inspect context, plan, edit code, and execute commands. The SDK also had context-management support such as compaction, intended to let work continue without immediately exhausting the context window.

### 2. Claude began implementation with an overly broad scope

In the early phase, Claude tended to try to build too much in a single pass. The article says it would “attempt to one-shot the app,” rather than breaking the work into smaller feature-by-feature increments.

Observable result: Claude began implementing a large amount of functionality in one context window.

### 3. The context window ran out mid-implementation

Often, according to the post, this broad implementation attempt caused Claude to run out of context “in the middle of its implementation.”

At that point, the project was left in an incomplete state: a feature could be “half-implemented and undocumented.” The article notes that this happened even with compaction enabled, because compaction did not always pass “perfectly clear instructions” to the next agent session.

### 4. A later Claude session resumed without enough usable context

After the previous session ended, a new agent instance started in a fresh context window. It did not have a complete memory of the prior session’s unfinished work.

The next Claude session found the codebase in a partially modified state, but the source says it had to “guess at what had happened.” Because the previous state was not clearly documented, the agent spent substantial time trying to restore or understand the basic app rather than making clean forward progress.

Observable feedback/signals available to the later session included the codebase state itself and whatever compaction summary had carried over, but the article says those signals were insufficiently clear in these cases.

### 5. The agent spent time recovering basic functionality

The later session then used time trying to get the app working again. The article describes this as spending “substantial time trying to get the basic app working again.”

The post does not provide a full command transcript for this failed run, but elsewhere in the same discussion it describes Claude as commonly making code changes and using tests or command-line checks such as unit tests or `curl` commands against a development server.

### 6. In later project stages, Claude sometimes stopped too early

Anthropic describes a second recurring pattern that happened later in projects. Once some features had already been built, a later Claude instance would inspect the repository, see that visible progress had been made, and “declare the job done.”

The source says this happened even though the app was not fully complete as a production-quality clone.

Observable sequence:

1. Some features existed in the project.
2. A fresh Claude session looked around the codebase.
3. It observed that progress had been made.
4. It concluded the task was complete.
5. It ended or reported completion despite remaining work.

### 7. Claude also marked features complete without full end-to-end verification

The article separately reports another observed failure mode around testing. Without explicit prompting, Claude would make code changes and sometimes run unit tests or `curl` checks against a development server.

However, the post says Claude would still fail to recognize that a feature did not work end-to-end. In other words, the tests or checks it performed were not always sufficient to reveal that the user-facing feature was broken.

For the web-app task, Anthropic reports that Claude performed better once explicitly prompted to use browser automation tools and test “as a human user would.” Claude used browser automation through Puppeteer MCP in these improved runs, including taking screenshots while testing the claude.ai clone.

### 8. Tooling limitations still left some bugs

Even after browser-based testing improved results, the post notes remaining limitations. For example, Claude could not see browser-native alert modals through Puppeteer MCP. Features relying on those modals “tended to be buggier as a result.”

Observable signal: the browser automation tooling did not expose every kind of browser UI state to Claude, so some issues were harder for it to observe during testing.

### 9. Final outcome in the unmodified harness

The article’s reported outcome is that, out of the box, Claude running in the SDK loop with only the high-level instruction did not reliably produce a production-quality clone of claude.ai.

The failure manifested as:

- early sessions attempting too much at once;
- context exhaustion during implementation;
- subsequent sessions inheriting half-implemented, undocumented work;
- later sessions sometimes declaring completion after seeing partial progress;
- features being marked complete after insufficient testing;
- some end-to-end bugs remaining difficult to detect because of tool/vision limitations.

Anthropic then presents a revised harness as a remedy: an initializer agent, a feature list, `init.sh`, `claude-progress.txt`, git commits, incremental coding-agent sessions, and explicit end-to-end testing. Those are described as improvements after observing the failure patterns, not as the original failed behavior itself.

Sources:

- [Anthropic — Effective harnesses for long-running agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents?lid=1f0n56CPItf3Nm9NR&utm_source=openai)
